3	Read this file and `graph/JOURNAL.md` at the start of every iteration, before choosing any work.
4	This file is owned by the user. The loop never edits it; propose changes in the journal instead.
5	
6	`graph/PLAN.md` is the design spec and the source of truth for what to build and why.
7	When something here seems arbitrary, read the matching section there before concluding anything.
8	
9	## Mission
10	
11	Build the macOS connection graph described in `graph/PLAN.md`, then keep improving it.
12	
13	It reads the user's own iMessage history and Contacts and draws the graph of everyone they know and how those people connect to each other.
14	It is a personal tool with exactly one user, never distributed.
15	"Done" does not end the loop. When the build completes, continue as a standing quality program over the same scope.
16	
17	## Hard constraints
18	
19	A violation is never an improvement, regardless of how good the idea looks.
20	
21	1. **`chat.db` is opened read-only and never written, copied, or moved.** `chat.db` runs in WAL mode with Messages writing continuously, and recent messages live in `chat.db-wal` until checkpointed. `?immutable=1` skips the WAL, silently missing the newest messages and misbehaving against a live writer, so it is banned on the live database. Open plain read-only, expect participation via the `-shm` sidecar, and retry on `SQLITE_BUSY`. Copying it would duplicate every message body ever sent.
22	2. **Message text is never persisted.** It is read transiently by the model pass; only derived guesses are stored. Never write message text to disk, to logs, to the journal, or to a commit.
23	3. **No real personal data in git, ever.** No message text, no phone numbers, no names, no exported graphs, no screenshots containing real contacts, no database copies. Add `graph/.gitignore` covering build output, extracted data, and any local cache before the first data-touching commit.
24	4. **Nothing is uploaded without explicit user authorization.** The model pass defaults to a local provider, so message snippets never leave the machine; configuring a cloud provider is the user's choice.
25	   Uploading derived graph data is banned unless the user explicitly authorizes a specific destination for a specific dataset; the loop never initiates or assumes such an authorization, and message text is never uploadable under any authorization (constraint 2 stands on its own).
26	   No telemetry, no analytics.
27	   Authorizations on record: 2026-07-31, the user authorized uploading derived graph exports (nodes and edges only, no message text) to the Haven Polygres project pa6ee1830f10557dcc9bfd0c, so the agent has a queryable store of the whole relationship network.
28	5. **Stay inside `graph/`.** This lives in the euno-app repo but shares nothing with Haven. Never modify `convex/`, `src/`, `ios/`, `CHANGELOG.md`, `package.json`, or any root config. Haven's CI, changelog, and version numbers are not yours.
29	6. **Never merge to main.** Open PRs; the user merges.
30	7. **No production surface anywhere.** No deploys, no publishing, no distribution, no notarization work. This is a local tool.
31	8. Global rules apply in full: plain ASCII everywhere, conventional commits, TDD for logic, no agent or tool names in commits or PR bodies, no co-author footers.
32	9. **Never edit this file.**
33	
34	## Standing blocked-on-user items
35	
36	Prepare, then wait. Track readiness in the journal.
37	
38	- Merging any PR.
39	- Choosing and funding a model provider or installing Ollama.
40	- Any decision that contradicts `PLAN.md` rather than refining it.
41	
42	## Each iteration
43	
44	1. Read `JOURNAL.md`, check `git status` and open PR state.
45	2. Pick the highest rung of the ladder below that has available work.
46	3. Do one coherent unit of work to completion: tested, verified, committed, pushed, PR opened or updated.
47	4. Update `JOURNAL.md`: done, in-flight, blocked, next intent.
48	5. Schedule the next wakeup per Pacing.
49	
50	## Priority ladder
51	
52	**P0. Repair.** Failing tests, broken builds, red CI. Before anything else.
53	
54	**P1. Babysit.** Open PRs: CI green, review comments addressed. Cap of 3 open PRs. At the cap, do commit-light work instead: self-review, journal planning, scratchpad experiments.
55	
56	**P2. Build, in the order given in PLAN.md.**
57	1. Extraction from `chat.db` and Contacts into a working model.
58	2. Identity resolution, names and photos from Contacts.
59	3. Non-person filter, tuned against real results.
60	4. Graph construction: nodes, edges, pruning.
61	5. Layout, render, assembly animation.
62	6. Interaction: focus, time filter, toggles.
63	7. Model pass for unnamed handles, asynchronous after render.
64	8. Persistence and resync.
65	9. Export.
66	
67	Step 5 is the first moment the tool is worth looking at. Everything before it is invisible plumbing. Get there fast.
68	
69	**P3. Tune against reality.** The filter thresholds, the group-liveness bar, the edge pruning, and the label density are all calibrated guesses. Measure them against the real database, report the numbers in the journal, and adjust. This rung stays open permanently and is the main reason the loop keeps earning its keep after the build.
70	
71	**P4. Quality passes.** Test depth, edge cases, accessibility, performance at ~700 nodes, animation feel, copy, refactors for clarity.
72	
73	**P5. Horizon check**, at most once per week of loop time. Re-verify assumptions that could rot: macOS schema changes, model provider pricing. Date it in the journal.
74	
75	If every rung is exhausted, extend P4. If that saturates, heartbeat rather than manufacture work.
76	Ideas outside this scope go in the journal as suggestions for the user, not into the code.
77	
78	## Quality bar
79	
80	A change qualifies only if all hold:
81	
82	- It fixes a named defect or closes a named gap, recorded in the journal entry.
83	- Logic changes follow TDD: failing test first, for the right reason, then implementation.
84	- Tests pass, including the Swift test target.
85	- No new dependency without a written reason.
86	- You would approve the diff as a reviewer with no context beyond the diff.
87	
88	Churn is not improvement: no renames for taste, no comment noise, no speculative abstraction, no reformatting passes.
89	An iteration that finds nothing qualifying says so in the journal and moves down the ladder. That is honest, not a failure.
90	
91	## Testing with real data
92	
93	Real data is available and is the only honest way to tune the filters.
94	But tests must be deterministic and must not depend on a database that changes daily.
95	
96	The split: **tune against real data, assert against fixtures.**
97	Build small synthetic fixtures covering the shapes that matter (shortcode, never-replied thread, degenerate 2-member group, multi-service duplicate handle, large group) and write assertions against those.
98	Use the real database for measurement and calibration, and report findings as numbers in the journal, never as committed data.
99	
100	## Workflow
101	
102	One worktree per branch under `.worktrees`, absolute paths in every command, `cd` per call.
103	This repo has a documented history of edits landing in the wrong copy because of persistent shell cwd. Take it seriously.
104	
105	Branch names: `graph/<topic>`.
106	PR bodies include a plain-language TLDR.
107	Never force-push main. Force-push only your own branches, and after an upstream squash-merge use `rebase --onto` rather than merging main in.
108	After the user merges, remove the worktree, delete the branch, journal it.
109	
110	## Pacing
111	
112	Self-pace with ScheduleWakeup, passing the same loop prompt through each time.
113	Actively working: continue immediately.
114	Waiting on CI or review only: 20 to 30 minutes.
115	Blocked everywhere or saturated: 60 minutes.
116	Never stop on your own initiative. The loop ends when the user says stop or usage runs out.
117	
118	## Journal discipline
119	
120	Newest entry first, one per iteration, timestamped.
121	Each entry: DONE with PR numbers, IN-FLIGHT with CI state, BLOCKED, NEXT intent, and any suggestion for the user.
122	Keep a short standing-state block at the top current.
123	Trim entries older than two weeks into a one-paragraph summary.
124	Numbers measured against the real database belong here. Real names and message content do not.
